column1: # ZAP API-scan rule tuning. SEPARATE from the baseline `rules.tsv` — this file
# is consumed by an OpenAPI-driven `zaproxy/action-api-scan` (or a manual
# `zap-api-scan.py`) run, not by the passive baseline crawl. See
# docs/security/api-testing.md for how the spec is generated and fed in.
# Format: <ruleId>\t<threshold>\t<comment>   (tab-separated)
# Thresholds: IGNORE | WARN | FAIL
#   (default: FAIL for HIGH/MEDIUM, WARN for LOW)
# Start strict: no rule is downgraded without a documented, owned reason below.
# The entries here are the ones an OpenAPI-driven active scan commonly trips on
# for a stateless JSON+JWT API where the alternative is worse than the alert.
# 10096  Timestamp Disclosure — the API returns ISO-8601 timestamps
#        (createdAt / deliveredAt / expiresAt) as first-class data. These are
#        not "leaked" secrets; they are the payload. WARN so a genuinely odd
#        timestamp still shows up in the report without failing the scan.

column3: Timestamps (createdAt/deliveredAt/…) are legitimate JSON response fields, not a disclosure.

column1: # 10015  Re-examine Cache-control Directives — only the public, cacheable
#        /widget/config route sets Cache-Control; authenticated JSON responses
#        are uncached by default. WARN rather than FAIL on this LOW-confidence
#        heuristic; tighten if an authed route starts advertising caching.

column3: Only the public widget bootstrap is cacheable; authed JSON is uncached. Low-value on a JSON API.

column1: # Everything else stays at ZAP defaults (FAIL on HIGH/MEDIUM). In particular,
# do NOT add IGNOREs for: SQL/NoSQL injection, path traversal, XXE, SSRF,
# auth-bypass, CORS misconfiguration, or missing-security-header rules — those
# are exactly what this scan exists to catch.
